title: Levothyroxine and Alcohol: Is It Safe? Synthroid, Dosing & Hangovers
excerpt: Can you drink on levothyroxine or Synthroid? How alcohol affects absorption, dosing routine, and thyroid levels, plus what to do the morning after a night out.
metaDescription: Can you drink on levothyroxine or Synthroid? How alcohol affects absorption, your dose routine, and thyroid levels, plus hangover-morning rules.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** for most people taking levothyroxine (Synthroid, Levoxyl, Unithroid, Euthyrox and generics), an occasional drink in moderation is generally considered acceptable. Major drug references don't list a strong direct chemical interaction between levothyroxine and alcohol the way they do for drugs like metronidazole or acetaminophen. The real problems are indirect. Drinking can throw off the strict routine levothyroxine depends on, a hangover morning is full of things that block its absorption (coffee, antacids, a big greasy breakfast, vomiting), and regular heavy drinking affects the thyroid and liver in ways that can make your dose harder to get right. Alcohol can also make the symptoms of an under- or over-treated thyroid feel worse or harder to recognize.

**The quick rules:** Keep taking your levothyroxine every day, including the morning after a night out. Take it the way you normally do, on an empty stomach with a full glass of water, and wait the usual 30 to 60 minutes before coffee or food. Keep calcium antacids like Tums, iron, and mineral-heavy drinks at least 4 hours away from your dose. If you vomit within an hour or so of taking it, or you miss a dose, don't double up on your own; check with your pharmacist. If you drink most days, tell the doctor who manages your thyroid, because it can affect your blood tests and your dose.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and label guidance about levothyroxine and alcohol. It is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history, your thyroid condition, and your full medication list. **Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before changing how or when you take levothyroxine.** **Get medical help promptly if** you have chest pain, a racing or irregular heartbeat that doesn't settle, severe shortness of breath, fainting, or confusion. Those can have many causes, including thyroid dose problems, and should not be written off as "just a hangover." In an emergency, call 911.

## How Levothyroxine and Alcohol Actually Interact

Levothyroxine is a man-made copy of **thyroxine (T4)**, the main hormone your thyroid gland produces. People take it when their own thyroid doesn't make enough hormone (hypothyroidism), after thyroid surgery or radioactive iodine treatment, and in some cases of thyroid nodules or thyroid cancer. Your body converts T4 into **T3**, the more active form, mostly in the liver, kidneys, and other tissues. That hormone sets the pace of your metabolism: heart rate, energy, body temperature, digestion, and mood all respond to it.

Levothyroxine is a fussy drug. It has a narrow therapeutic range, which means the gap between too little and too much is fairly small, and doctors adjust doses in small steps based on blood tests. It's also absorbed unevenly. A fair share of each tablet never makes it into your bloodstream, and anything that changes how much gets absorbed can nudge your thyroid levels up or down.

Alcohol doesn't attack levothyroxine directly. Instead it affects the drug in four indirect ways:

1. **Absorption.** Levothyroxine is absorbed in the small intestine and needs an empty stomach. Vomiting, diarrhea, and the hangover-breakfast staples (coffee, antacids, rich food) can all cut how much of the dose you absorb.
2. **Routine.** The drug works best when you take it at the same time and in the same way every day. A late night is one of the most common reasons people skip, forget, or mistime a dose.
3. **The thyroid itself.** Regular heavy drinking has been linked in research to changes in thyroid hormone levels and even thyroid size. That can muddy the picture your doctor sees on blood tests.
4. **Symptoms.** Alcohol and hangovers cause fatigue, low mood, poor sleep, a fast heartbeat, and shakiness. Those overlap with the symptoms of a thyroid dose that's too low or too high, which makes it harder to tell what's going on.

None of these is dramatic on its own after one or two drinks. They matter more if you drink heavily, drink often, or your thyroid levels are still being adjusted.

## Synthroid and Alcohol: Is the Brand Any Different?

**Synthroid is levothyroxine.** So are Levoxyl, Unithroid, Euthyrox, Tirosint (a gel capsule and liquid form), and the many generic tablets. The active ingredient is identical, so everything in this guide about alcohol applies equally to Synthroid and to generic levothyroxine.

There are two small differences worth knowing:

- **Inactive ingredients vary.** Different brands use different fillers and dyes. That doesn't change how they interact with alcohol, but it's one reason many doctors prefer you stay on the same product rather than switching back and forth. Small differences in how each product is absorbed can shift your levels.
- **Liquid and gel forms may be less sensitive to stomach conditions.** Tirosint and the oral solutions are designed to dissolve without relying as much on stomach acid. Some doctors use them for people with absorption problems. If you find your levels are hard to keep steady and you drink or take acid reducers, it's a fair question to raise with your doctor.

If you're on Synthroid, the safe-drinking advice is the same: moderate amounts, keep the dose routine steady, and keep absorption blockers away from your dose.

## Is It Safe to Drink Alcohol on Levothyroxine?

For most people with well-controlled hypothyroidism, light to moderate drinking is not considered dangerous. US dietary guidance defines moderate drinking as up to one drink a day for women and up to two for men, and many health bodies now say less is better. Levothyroxine doesn't make a standard drink more intoxicating, and it doesn't cause a reaction like the flushing, vomiting, and racing heart some antibiotics cause.

Where caution matters more:

- **You've just started levothyroxine or recently changed dose.** Your doctor is trying to read your blood tests and symptoms to find the right dose. Heavy drinking adds noise to both. It's a sensible time to keep drinking light.
- **You have heart disease or an irregular heartbeat.** Too much thyroid hormone and too much alcohol can both speed up the heart and trigger rhythm problems such as atrial fibrillation. Together they deserve more care, especially in older adults.
- **You have liver disease.** The liver helps convert T4 to T3 and makes the proteins that carry thyroid hormone in the blood. Liver damage from alcohol can change thyroid test results and how the hormone behaves.
- **You take other medicines that interact with alcohol.** Many people on levothyroxine also take antidepressants, sleep aids, blood pressure medicines, or diabetes drugs. Those interactions are often more significant than the thyroid one.
- **You've had thyroid cancer.** Some people on levothyroxine after thyroid cancer are kept on deliberately higher doses to suppress TSH (the pituitary hormone that tells the thyroid to grow). Their margin for heart-related side effects can be smaller, so it's worth asking the specialist directly.

If you drink most days, or have several drinks at a time on a regular basis, that's worth telling your doctor plainly. It isn't about judgment. It's information they need to interpret your blood work and set your dose.

## The Morning After: Taking Levothyroxine With a Hangover

This is where most real problems happen. A hangover morning tends to break almost every levothyroxine rule at once. Here's how to keep your dose on track.

### Do take your dose

Don't skip levothyroxine because you feel rough. Missing one dose isn't an emergency, because T4 has a long half-life (roughly a week), so levels fall slowly. But making a habit of skipping weekend doses adds up, and consistency is the whole game with this drug.

### Take it the usual way

- **On an empty stomach**, with a full glass of plain water.
- **Wait 30 to 60 minutes** before eating or drinking anything other than water. Follow whatever timing your doctor or label gave you.
- **Swallow it whole** with water rather than with juice, coffee, or a sports drink.

### Watch the coffee

Coffee is a well-documented absorption blocker for levothyroxine. Studies have shown that taking the tablet with espresso or drip coffee lowers how much is absorbed. After a night out, coffee is usually the first thing people reach for. Take your tablet with water first, then wait before the coffee.

### Keep antacids and minerals away from your dose

This is the most important hangover-specific rule. Several common hangover remedies bind to levothyroxine in the gut and stop it being absorbed:

- **Calcium antacids** such as Tums (calcium carbonate)
- **Magnesium and aluminum antacids** such as Maalox, Mylanta, and milk of magnesia
- **Iron supplements** and multivitamins with iron or calcium
- **Mineral-heavy electrolyte drinks and powders** that contain calcium or magnesium
- **Sucralfate** and some cholesterol-lowering powders, if you take them

The usual advice is to separate these from levothyroxine by **at least 4 hours**. If heartburn wakes you up the morning after, it's better to take your levothyroxine, wait, and treat the heartburn later, or ask your pharmacist about an option that won't clash. We cover the antacid side in more detail in [Tums and alcohol](/never-hungover/tums-and-alcohol).

### Acid reducers are a slower problem

Proton pump inhibitors such as omeprazole and, to a smaller extent, H2 blockers such as famotidine lower stomach acid. Levothyroxine tablets dissolve better in an acidic stomach, so regular use of acid reducers has been linked to people needing a higher levothyroxine dose. A single tablet after a night of heartburn isn't a big deal. Taking them every day is something your doctor should know about.

### A big greasy breakfast

Food in general reduces levothyroxine absorption, and high-fiber foods, soy, and some fruit juices are known to interfere. That's why the wait before breakfast matters. If you eat right after the tablet one morning, the effect on a single dose is modest. Doing it routinely can lower your levels over time.

## What If You Vomit After Taking Levothyroxine?

Vomiting is one of the clearest ways a hangover can cost you a dose.

- **If you vomit soon after taking it** (within roughly the first hour), some or most of the dose may not have been absorbed.
- **If you vomit several hours later**, most of it has likely already been absorbed.

There isn't a single universal rule for re-dosing, and advice differs between pharmacists and countries. Because levothyroxine lasts a long time in the body, a single partly lost dose usually matters little. **Don't take a second tablet on your own.** Call your pharmacist, tell them when you took the dose and when you vomited, and follow what they say. If you are vomiting repeatedly and can't keep anything down, including water, that's a reason to seek medical care in its own right, because dehydration can become serious.

## What If You Forgot Your Dose After a Night Out?

Most levothyroxine labels say that if you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember, unless it's almost time for the next one. In that case, skip the missed dose and go back to your normal schedule. Don't take two doses at once unless your doctor or pharmacist has told you that's fine for you; some doctors are comfortable with it for this drug, others aren't, so ask once and keep the answer.

A few habits make missed doses less likely:

- **Keep the bottle next to something you always do**, like your toothbrush or phone charger.
- **Use a weekly pill organizer**, so you can see at a glance whether today's dose is gone.
- **Set a phone reminder** that doesn't depend on remembering after a late night.

### Bedtime dosing as an option

Some people find a morning dose hard to protect, especially if they work shifts or often have late nights. A randomized trial from the Netherlands, published in 2010, found that taking levothyroxine at bedtime (several hours after the last meal) worked at least as well as morning dosing for thyroid levels. Some doctors now offer bedtime dosing as an option. It is not a good idea to switch on your own, and it doesn't solve the drinking question: taking your tablet right after a night of drinks and bar snacks wouldn't meet the "empty stomach" rule either. But if your mornings are chaotic, it's worth asking your doctor whether a different timing would suit you better.

## How Heavy Drinking Affects the Thyroid

This section is about patterns of regular, heavy drinking, not an occasional night out.

Research on alcohol and the thyroid shows a few consistent themes, though the details are still debated:

- **Alcohol may act on the thyroid gland directly.** Studies in heavy drinkers have reported lower levels of thyroid hormones and, in some cases, a smaller thyroid gland. Levels often move back toward normal after a period without alcohol.
- **It can blunt the body's thyroid signaling.** Chronic heavy drinking has been reported to dampen the pituitary's response to TRH, one of the hormones that controls the thyroid. That can make standard blood tests harder to interpret.
- **The liver matters.** The liver converts T4 to T3 and produces thyroid-binding proteins. Alcohol-related liver disease can change these, which shifts test results in ways that don't always reflect how much hormone your tissues are actually getting.
- **Moderate drinking and autoimmune thyroid disease is a surprising wrinkle.** A Danish population study published around 2012 found that people who drank moderately had a lower risk of developing autoimmune hypothyroidism than non-drinkers. This is an observational finding, which means it shows an association, not cause and effect. It is not a reason to start drinking, and it says nothing about people who already take levothyroxine.

For more background on how alcohol affects the thyroid and other hormones, see our guide on [alcohol and thyroid health](/never-hungover/alcohol-thyroid-hormonal-disruption-2025).

The practical takeaway is simple. If you drink heavily on a regular basis and your thyroid levels keep bouncing around or your dose keeps changing, alcohol may be part of the reason, and your doctor needs to know.

## Hangover or Thyroid Problem? Overlapping Symptoms

One reason this topic is confusing is that alcohol and thyroid dose problems produce similar feelings.

| Symptom | Could be the hangover | Could be the thyroid dose |
|---|---|---|
| Fatigue, sluggishness, brain fog | Common hangover symptom | Typical of too little thyroid hormone |
| Low mood | Common the day after drinking | Typical of too little thyroid hormone |
| Racing or pounding heart | Common after drinking | Can mean too much thyroid hormone |
| Shakiness or tremor | Common after heavy drinking | Can mean too much thyroid hormone |
| Poor sleep | Alcohol disrupts sleep | Can mean too much thyroid hormone |
| Feeling hot and sweaty | Common after drinking | Can mean too much thyroid hormone |
| Weight gain | Alcohol is high in calories | Typical of too little thyroid hormone |

A hangover should fade within a day or so. If these symptoms hang around for days, keep showing up when you haven't been drinking, or are getting worse over weeks, that points away from the hangover and toward something your doctor should check, often with a simple blood test.

The racing heart deserves a special mention. Both alcohol and too much thyroid hormone can trigger a fast or irregular heartbeat. If you notice a heartbeat that feels chaotic or doesn't settle with rest, get it checked. Our article on [heart racing after drinking](/never-hungover/heart-racing-after-drinking) covers the alcohol side of this in more depth.

## Levothyroxine, Alcohol, and Weight

Many people on levothyroxine are watching their weight, because an underactive thyroid tends to slow metabolism and weight loss can feel slow even once levels are back to normal.

Levothyroxine is not a weight-loss drug, and taking more than prescribed to lose weight is dangerous. Alcohol, meanwhile, works against weight goals in several ways. It carries about 7 calories per gram, comes packaged with sugary mixers, lowers inhibitions around late-night food, and disrupts sleep, which affects hunger hormones the next day. If you're frustrated that your weight isn't moving on levothyroxine, cutting back on alcohol is one of the simpler levers you can pull, and it also helps keep your dosing routine steady.

## A Simple Plan If You Take Levothyroxine and Drink

Here's a practical routine that respects both the drug and real life:

1. **Before you go out:** Decide on a limit. Eat a proper meal. Put tomorrow's tablet and a glass by your bed or next to your toothbrush.
2. **During the night:** Alternate alcoholic drinks with water. Drinking on an empty stomach makes you feel drunk faster and worse the next day; see our guide on [drinking on an empty stomach](/never-hungover/drinking-on-an-empty-stomach) for why.
3. **The next morning:** Take your levothyroxine first, with plain water, on an empty stomach.
4. **Wait** your usual 30 to 60 minutes before coffee or breakfast.
5. **Keep antacids, iron, calcium, and mineral drinks** at least 4 hours from your dose.
6. **If you vomit soon after the dose or forget it**, call your pharmacist rather than guessing.
7. **Over the longer term**, tell your doctor roughly how much you drink, especially before blood tests or a dose change.

## Who Should Be Most Careful

You should talk to your doctor before drinking, or about how much you drink, if you:

- Have **heart disease, atrial fibrillation, or a history of palpitations**
- Have **liver disease** or have been told your liver enzymes are raised
- Have recently **started levothyroxine or changed dose**
- Take levothyroxine at **TSH-suppressing doses after thyroid cancer**
- Are **pregnant or trying to get pregnant**, when thyroid levels need especially close control and alcohol is best avoided
- Take **other medicines** with their own alcohol warnings, such as antidepressants, sleep medicines, opioids, or diabetes drugs
- Drink **most days** or **binge regularly**

A five-minute conversation with a pharmacist who can see your full medication list is often the quickest way to get a clear answer. For a broader look at how common drugs interact with supplements and alcohol, see our [DHM medication interactions and safety guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025).

## What About Hangover Supplements and Levothyroxine?

People on levothyroxine often ask whether hangover supplements are safe to take. The honest answer is that very few have been studied alongside levothyroxine, so the safest approach is about **timing and ingredients**.

- **Check for minerals.** Many hangover and "recovery" products contain calcium, magnesium, zinc, or iron. Those can bind levothyroxine in the gut, so keep them at least 4 hours from your dose, the same as antacids.
- **Separate everything from your thyroid tablet.** The simplest rule is that levothyroxine goes in alone, with water, on an empty stomach. Anything else, including supplements, waits.
- **DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree that's studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver. Most of the evidence comes from animal and lab studies, with limited human data. There's no good evidence that DHM prevents hangovers outright, and there are no published studies of DHM taken alongside levothyroxine. Lab studies suggest DHM may affect some drug-metabolizing enzymes, which is a reason to ask your pharmacist before adding it. If you do try it, take it in the evening with your drinks or before bed, so it's well away from a morning levothyroxine dose. Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much to take and when.

If you get the all-clear and want to try one, two popular options are [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20), a simple, low-cost choice (note it lists electrolytes and minerals, which is another reason to keep it hours away from your thyroid tablet), and [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20), which adds L-cysteine and other ingredients. No supplement replaces the basics: drinking less, eating, staying hydrated, and keeping your levothyroxine routine steady. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) walks through the habits with the best evidence.

## The Bottom Line

- There's no strong direct chemical interaction between levothyroxine (or Synthroid) and alcohol, and moderate drinking is generally considered acceptable for people with well-controlled thyroid levels.
- The real risks are indirect: missed or mistimed doses, poor absorption on hangover mornings, and the effect of regular heavy drinking on the thyroid, liver, and heart.
- Take your dose every day, on an empty stomach with water, and wait before coffee or food.
- Keep Tums and other antacids, iron, calcium, and mineral drinks or supplements at least 4 hours from your dose.
- Don't double up after vomiting or a missed dose without checking with your pharmacist.
- If you drink most days, have heart or liver problems, or your levels keep changing, talk to your doctor.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you drink alcohol while taking levothyroxine?**

For most people with well-controlled thyroid levels, moderate drinking is generally considered acceptable. Major drug references don't list a strong direct interaction between levothyroxine and alcohol. The bigger issues are indirect: drinking can lead to missed or mistimed doses, hangover mornings bring coffee, antacids, and vomiting that reduce absorption, and regular heavy drinking can affect the thyroid, liver, and heart. If you drink most days or have heart or liver problems, talk to your doctor.

**Is it okay to drink alcohol on Synthroid?**

Synthroid is a brand of levothyroxine, so the same advice applies. Moderate drinking is generally considered acceptable for people whose thyroid levels are stable. Keep taking your dose every day on an empty stomach with water, keep antacids and mineral supplements at least 4 hours away, and tell your doctor if you drink regularly or heavily.

**Should I take levothyroxine the morning after drinking?**

Yes. Don't skip it because you're hungover. Take it as usual with a full glass of plain water on an empty stomach, then wait your normal 30 to 60 minutes before coffee or breakfast. Keep Tums, other antacids, iron, calcium, and mineral-heavy electrolyte drinks at least 4 hours away from the dose.

**What should I do if I throw up after taking levothyroxine?**

If you vomit soon after the dose, some of it may not have been absorbed. If it was several hours later, most of it probably was. Because levothyroxine lasts a long time in the body, one partly lost dose usually matters little. Don't take a second tablet on your own; call your pharmacist and follow their advice. If you can't keep any fluids down, seek medical care.

**Can alcohol affect my thyroid blood tests?**

Regular heavy drinking has been linked to changes in thyroid hormone levels and in how the body controls the thyroid, and alcohol-related liver disease can change thyroid test results. An occasional drink is unlikely to matter much. If you drink most days, tell your doctor, because it can affect how they read your results and set your dose.

**Can I take Tums for a hangover if I'm on levothyroxine?**

You can, but not close to your dose. Calcium carbonate antacids like Tums can bind levothyroxine in the gut and reduce how much you absorb. The usual advice is to separate them by at least 4 hours. The same applies to magnesium or aluminum antacids, iron, calcium supplements, and mineral-heavy electrolyte drinks.

**Is DHM safe to take with levothyroxine?**

There are no published studies of DHM taken with levothyroxine, so ask your pharmacist first. Lab studies suggest DHM may affect some drug-metabolizing enzymes, and many DHM and hangover products contain minerals that can block levothyroxine absorption. If you're cleared to try it, take it in the evening, well away from a morning levothyroxine dose.

**Does alcohol make hypothyroid symptoms worse?**

It can make them feel worse. Alcohol and hangovers cause fatigue, low mood, poor sleep, and weight gain, which overlap with symptoms of an underactive thyroid. Alcohol can also cause a racing heart and shakiness, which overlap with signs of too much thyroid hormone. If symptoms last for days or show up when you haven't been drinking, ask your doctor to check your levels.
